notes.title: 그립다 vs 보고 싶다
notes.text: 보고 싶어요 is the everyday "I miss you / I want to see you." 그리워요 is deeper and a little literary — a longing for someone or something far away or in the past: 고향이 그리워요 "I long for home." Korean songs are full of 그리움 (longing).

notes.title: 짜증 나!
notes.text: 짜증 나 (I'm annoyed!) is one of the most common lines in Korean dramas. 화나다 means to get angry; 열 받다 is slang for "to be steamed." A gentle way to ask what's wrong: 무슨 일 있어? or 기분이 안 좋아?

notes.title: -거든요
notes.text: -거든(요) adds the background: "…you see." It's the most natural way to explain yourself: 늦었어요. 버스가 안 왔거든요. (I'm late. The bus didn't come, you see.) It never starts a conversation — it explains something already said.

notes.title: -아/어하다
notes.text: Feeling adjectives describe your own feelings: 기뻐요 (I'm glad). To describe someone else's visible feelings, add -아/어하다: 기쁘다 → 기뻐하다 (he's glad), 슬프다 → 슬퍼하다, 부럽다 → 부러워하다. And 사과하다 (to apologize) has a twin: 사과 also means "apple"!

notes.title: Taking a compliment
notes.text: Koreans often wave compliments away: 아니에요! (Not at all!) or 별말씀을요 (Don't mention it). Favorite compliments: 착하다 (kind, good-hearted), 똑똑하다 (smart), 매력 있다 (charming), 인상이 좋다 (has a kind face), 성격이 좋다 (has a nice personality).
